title: Best Time to Visit Kashmir: A Season-by-Season Guide
excerpt: Snow in Gulmarg, tulips in Srinagar or green meadows in Pahalgam – here is what each season in Kashmir looks like and how to choose the right month for your trip.
body: Kashmir changes completely from one season to the next, so the 'best' time really depends on what you want to see. Here is a simple guide to help you choose.
Spring (March to May): tulips and fresh green valleys

Spring is when the valley wakes up. Almond and apple trees blossom, the snow on the higher slopes starts to melt, and Srinagar's tulip garden usually opens for a few weeks around late March and April (exact dates depend on the weather each year). Days are pleasant and nights are still cool, so carry a light jacket.
Summer (June to August): meadows, lakes and long days

Summer is the most popular time for families. Sonamarg, Pahalgam and Gulmarg are green and easy to explore, shikara rides on Dal Lake are at their best in the long evenings, and the weather in the hills stays comfortable even when the plains are hot. It is also peak season, so book hotels and houseboats early.
Autumn (September to November): golden chinar trees

Autumn is a favourite with photographers. The chinar trees in the Mughal Gardens turn red and gold, the skies are clear and the crowds are smaller than in summer. Mornings and nights get cold from late October.
Winter (December to February): snow and skiing

If you want snow, come in winter. Gulmarg becomes a ski destination and the Gondola rides offer views of snow-covered peaks. Roads to Sonamarg and Pahalgam can close after heavy snowfall, so keep a day or two of flexibility in your plan and pack proper woollens.
Keep one buffer day – mountain roads and flights can be affected by weather.
Only postpaid mobile connections from other states work in Jammu & Kashmir.
Local taxi unions operate in Pahalgam and Gulmarg for some sightseeing points; these are usually paid locally.

title: Kerala for First-Timers: Hills, Spices, Backwaters and Beaches
excerpt: How to plan a first trip to Kerala – where to stay, how many nights to give each place and why a houseboat night is worth it.
body: Kerala packs a lot of variety into a small state: tea-covered hills, spice plantations, quiet backwaters and long beaches. A classic first trip takes six to eight days and moves from the hills down to the coast.
Munnar: tea gardens and cool air

Most trips start from Kochi and climb to Munnar. Two nights here give you time for the tea gardens and tea museum, a viewpoint or two and, in season, Eravikulam National Park. The drive up passes several waterfalls worth a short stop.

A night in Thekkady lets you walk through a spice plantation, see how cardamom and pepper grow, and take a boat ride on Periyar Lake. Evenings are a good time for a Kathakali or martial-arts performance.
Alleppey: a night on a houseboat

The backwaters are best experienced from a houseboat. You board around noon, cruise past villages and paddy fields, eat freshly cooked Kerala meals on board and anchor for the night. It is slow travel at its best – no driving, just the water.
Kovalam or Varkala: ending at the beach
Finish with two nights by the sea near Thiruvananthapuram. Kovalam has calm bays and lighthouse views; the city's Padmanabhaswamy Temple is close by (a strict dress code applies).
September to March is the most comfortable time for sightseeing.
June to August is monsoon – lush and cheaper, with Ayurveda treatments popular, but some activities can be affected by rain.
Christmas and New Year are peak weeks for houseboats and beach hotels.

title: North Goa or South Goa? How to Choose Where to Stay
excerpt: Lively beaches and nightlife or quiet sands and long walks – a simple comparison of North and South Goa to help you pick the right base.
body: Goa is small, but where you stay changes the feel of your holiday. Here is a quick comparison of the two halves of the coast.
North Goa: busy, lively and full of choice

Calangute, Baga, Candolim and Anjuna are where most first-time visitors stay. You will find water sports, beach shacks, markets, cafés and nightlife within a short drive, plus forts such as Aguada and Chapora. It is great for friends and families who want plenty to do – but beaches get crowded in peak season.
South Goa: calm, clean and relaxed

Colva, Benaulim, Varca and Palolem are quieter, with wide beaches, fewer crowds and a slower pace. It suits couples, honeymooners and anyone who wants to read, swim and walk on the sand. Evenings are calmer and resorts are more spread out.
The churches of Old Goa, including the Basilica of Bom Jesus (UNESCO-listed).
The colourful Latin Quarter of Fontainhas in Panjim.
A sunset at Fort Aguada or the Cabo de Rama cliffs.

For a first trip of four or five nights, split your stay: two or three nights in the North for sightseeing and fun, and two nights in the South to relax before you fly home. October to March has the best weather; the monsoon months are green and quiet, but the sea is not safe for swimming.

title: Char Dham Yatra: A Practical Planning Guide
excerpt: Registration, route, fitness, what to pack and how to choose between road and helicopter – everything to plan a smooth Char Dham Yatra.
body: The Char Dham Yatra to Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath is one of the most important pilgrimages in India. Good planning makes it safer and far more peaceful.

The temples usually open around Akshaya Tritiya (April or May) and close around Diwali (October or November). Exact dates are announced each year. May–June and September–October are the most comfortable months; heavy monsoon rains in July and August can cause landslides and delays.
Every pilgrim must register with the Uttarakhand government (online or at registration counters) before the yatra. Keep the registration and an ID with you at all times – it is checked on the route.
By road: about 9–10 nights from Haridwar, with treks of roughly 6 km at Yamunotri and 16–18 km at Kedarnath (ponies, palkis and pithus are available).
Do Dham (Kedarnath and Badrinath only): about 5–6 nights by road.
By helicopter: the four Dhams in about six days from Dehradun, with strict weight and baggage limits.

Kedarnath is at about 3,583 m. Start walking daily a few weeks before you travel, and consult your doctor if you have heart, lung or blood-pressure conditions. Go slowly, drink plenty of water and rest if you feel breathless or dizzy.
Warm layers, rain jacket, comfortable walking shoes and a walking stick.
Personal medicines, ORS, a small torch and a power bank.
Copies of ID and your yatra registration.

title: Andaman Island Hopping: Port Blair, Havelock and Neil Explained
excerpt: How ferries work, how many nights to spend on each island and which beaches to keep for sunrise and sunset in the Andamans.
body: Most Andaman holidays combine three islands: Port Blair for history, Havelock (Swaraj Dweep) for famous beaches, and Neil (Shaheed Dweep) for quiet village life. Here is how to plan the hops.

All flights land in Port Blair. Spend your first evening at the Cellular Jail, now a national memorial, and its light and sound show. If you have an extra day, take a boat to Ross Island and North Bay.

Give Havelock at least two nights. Radhanagar Beach is one of the most beautiful in Asia, especially at sunset. Elephant Beach, reached by boat, is the place for snorkelling over the coral reef; scuba diving and sea walks are available for those who want more.
Neil is small enough to cycle around. See the natural rock bridge at low tide, watch sunrise at Sitapur and sunset at Laxmanpur, and swim in the shallow water at Bharatpur Beach.
Private catamarans and government ferries link Port Blair, Havelock and Neil; the crossings take about 1–2 hours.
Ferries are booked once your flight times are confirmed and can be rescheduled in rough weather.
Carry a photo ID for every ferry and for Ross Island.
October to May has calm seas and clear water. The monsoon (June to September) brings rough seas and possible ferry cancellations.

title: Your First Trip to Ladakh: Altitude, Permits and Packing
excerpt: Why the first day in Leh is for rest, which places need permits and what to pack for Nubra Valley and Pangong Lake.
body: Ladakh is unforgettable – high passes, monasteries, sand dunes and blue lakes. Because Leh is at about 3,500 m, a little preparation makes a big difference to how much you enjoy it.

If you fly into Leh, spend the first day resting so your body can adjust to the altitude. Drink water, avoid alcohol and heavy exercise, and walk slowly. Altitude sickness (AMS) can affect anyone, however fit; consult a doctor before travel if you have heart, lung or blood-pressure conditions.
Indian visitors need an Inner Line Permit and environment fees for areas such as Nubra Valley and Pangong Lake. These are arranged in Leh before you set out; keep copies of your ID handy.
Leh and nearby monasteries (Thiksey, Hemis, Shey) in the first two days.
Over Khardung La to Nubra Valley – sand dunes at Hunder and Diskit Monastery.
Pangong Lake, famous for its changing shades of blue.
Warm layers even in summer, a windproof jacket, cap, sunglasses and strong sunscreen.
Lip balm, moisturiser and a reusable water bottle.
Basic medicines – talk to your doctor about altitude medication.
May to September is the main season when the high passes are open. Only postpaid mobile connections work in the region, and snow or landslides can close roads at short notice.

title: Planning Your First Rajasthan Trip: Three Easy Route Ideas
excerpt: Jaipur for a weekend, a week of forts and lakes, or the full desert circuit – three ways to see Rajasthan depending on your time.
body: Rajasthan is big, and distances between cities are long. Choosing a route that fits your days is the key to a relaxed trip. Here are three ideas.
The Pink City is easy to reach and full of sights: Amber Fort, Jal Mahal, City Palace, Jantar Mantar and the famous facade of Hawa Mahal. End a day at Nahargarh Fort for sunset over the city.

Jaipur, then Jodhpur's huge Mehrangarh Fort and blue old town, and finally Udaipur, the city of lakes, with its City Palace and boat rides on Lake Pichola. The drive from Jodhpur to Udaipur passes the beautiful Ranakpur Jain Temple.
Add Jaisalmer and a night at a desert camp near the Sam sand dunes – camel rides at sunset, folk music and dinner under the stars – to the forts-and-lakes route.
October to March is the best time; summers are very hot.
Distances are long – a private car with a driver is the most comfortable way to travel.
Many forts involve walking and steps; wear comfortable shoes.

title: Honeymoon Destinations in India for Every Season
excerpt: Snowy hills, houseboats, island beaches or desert palaces – a month-by-month guide to choosing your honeymoon destination in India.
body: The right honeymoon destination depends on when you get married. Here is a simple season-by-season guide to the most popular choices in India.
October to February: beaches, backwaters and snow
Andaman Islands – calm seas, white beaches and sunsets at Radhanagar.
Kerala – a private houseboat night on the backwaters and tea hills in Munnar.
Goa – South Goa's quiet beaches for a relaxed start to married life.
Manali or Gulmarg – for couples who dream of snow (December to February).
Rajasthan – palaces, lake views in Udaipur and a desert camp under the stars.
Kashmir – tulips and blossom in spring, green meadows in early summer.
Shimla and Manali – pleasant weather and mountain views.
Darjeeling and Gangtok – tea gardens, monasteries and Kanchenjunga sunrises.

The monsoon is a quieter, often better-value time. Kerala is lush and green, Ladakh is in its main season, and Udaipur's lakes fill up. Avoid island and beach trips with sea crossings during heavy rains.
Ask for a honeymoon cake, flower decoration and a candle-light dinner – many of our honeymoon packages include them, and we can add them to other trips on request.
